posts.body: Welcome to LIME — de whole Caribbean, one yard. 🌴 Whether you're home on the rock or living abroad, this is your space to link up, share, and big up each other. Tell us where you're from in the comments!
Sunday lunch question for the yard: what's the one dish that tastes like home to you? Pelau, oil down, rice and peas, cou-cou and flying fish, pepperpot… drop yours below. 🍲
Doubles debate time. 🌶️ Slight pepper, heavy pepper, or no pepper at all? And who makes the best doubles outside of Trinidad — share your spot so the diaspora can find it.
Living abroad but missing de sounds? Share the soca, reggae, dancehall, kompa, zouk or calypso tune you play when you need a little piece of home. 🎶 Check the Culture tab to post full tracks too.

Carnival season is coming. 🎭 Trinidad & Tobago Carnival is Monday and Tuesday, February 8–9, 2027, and Dominica's carnival season runs January 9 to February 10. Who's playing mas this year? Check Linkup for dates.
For everyone in the diaspora: the Roots tab lets you build your family tree privately — names, places and years, all in one spot. Start with your grandparents and see how far back you can go. 🌳
Our grandparents carried stories across the water — Anansi, Papa Bois, the soucouyant, duppy tales on the veranda. What story did your family tell you growing up? Share it in Culture → Stories. 📖
Looking for work, or hiring? The Wuk tab has job listings and links to Caribbean job boards. If you run a Caribbean-owned business, post your openings and help a cousin out. 💼

culture_poems.title: The Tropics in New York
culture_poems.body:
Bananas ripe and green, and ginger-root,
Cocoa in pods and alligator pears,
And tangerines and mangoes and grape fruit,
Fit for the highest prize at parish fairs,

Set in the window, bringing memories
Of fruit-trees laden by low-singing rills,
And dewy dawns, and mystical blue skies
In benediction over nun-like hills.

My eyes grew dim, and I could no more gaze;
A wave of longing through my body swept,
And, hungry for the old, familiar ways,
I turned aside and bowed my head and wept.

— Claude McKay (Jamaica), 1920 · public domain

culture_stories.title: Anansi the Spider
culture_stories.body: The clever spider of West African and Caribbean folklore, who wins by wit instead of strength. Every island has its own Anansi stories.

culture_stories.title: Papa Bois
culture_stories.body: Trinidad & Tobago's guardian of the forest and its animals — part man, part beast, and not someone hunters want to cross.

culture_stories.title: The Soucouyant
culture_stories.body: The fireball spirit of Eastern Caribbean folklore — an old woman by day who sheds her skin at night. Count the rice grains!
